strengths: Novel application of neural fields to general relativity with well-motivated Sobolev training using Jacobian/Hessian supervision achieving 10-10^5× accuracy improvements over finite differences
Exceptionally comprehensive technical treatment with rigorous mathematical foundation and thorough experimental validation on canonical GR solutions (Schwarzschild, Kerr, linearized gravity)
Impressive compression factors (1000-4000×) with high precision (1E-8 relative error) and useful JAX-based differential geometry library enabling automatic differentiation of physical quantities
Excellent presentation with clear pipeline description, multiple coordinate systems tested, and diverse downstream applications (geodesics, curvature tensors, Weyl scalars, Kretschmann invariants)
Rigorous validation methodology including coordinate-independent scalar invariants and reconstruction of seminal GR test cases (perihelion precession, ring singularities, gravitational wave effects)
weaknesses: Critical scope limitation: Only demonstrated on analytical solutions (Schwarzschild, Kerr, linearized gravity), not on actual numerical relativity simulations despite stated motivation of 'computationally intensive four-dimensional numerical simulations'; raises questions about practical utility

Accuracy saturation at ~1E-8 MAE cannot be exceeded despite FLOAT64, SOAP optimizer, and extensive tuning; error accumulation in geodesic rollouts (Figure 12) shows significant divergence, especially for complex Kerr orbits; accuracy degradation near singularities unresolved

Fundamental coordinate-system sensitivity (Table 9 shows 3 orders of magnitude variation across coordinates) remains unaddressed despite acknowledgment; conflicts with coordinate-independence claims in GR; distortion decomposition is coordinate-specific regularization, not general principle

Unclear practical advantages: Spectral methods are acknowledged to be 1000-5000× more efficient than finite differences yet no comparison provided; dense grid comparison is weak baseline; use case for metric weight storage vs. direct simulation output unclear

Severely limited experimental scope: Only vacuum solutions (no matter), static/simple-periodic dynamics (no binary mergers or complex evolution), small domains (r ∈ [3,14] for Kerr), single timeslices for most tests; no demonstration on realistic numerical relativity scenarios

Optimization fragility requiring SOAP optimizer (100× improvement over ADAM) and GradNorm weighting; Hessian supervision counterintuitively harms geodesic accuracy; suggests unresolved challenges in objective landscape not fully understood
Floating-point precision overhead: FLOAT64 required for geodesics despite FLOAT32 training negates compression advantages; reduces applicability for bandwidth/memory-constrained settings

strengths: Novel application of neural fields to computational general relativity with strong motivation addressing real storage challenges in NR
Technically sound methodology combining Sobolev training, distortion decomposition, and automatic differentiation for tensor fields
Comprehensive experimental validation including analytical solutions (Schwarzschild, Kerr, GWs) and realistic NR data (oscillating neutron star with BSSN)
Impressive empirical results: 4000× compression maintaining 5-7 decimal accuracy; derivatives 10⁵× more accurate than 6th-order finite differencing
Successful reconstruction of complex GR phenomena (perihelion precession, orbital dynamics, GW extraction, ring deformations) with ray-traced rendering
Excellent reproducibility with detailed specifications, promised open-source library, and thorough mathematical background
Well-presented with clear writing, intuitive figures, and balanced main text/appendix organization
weaknesses: Limited NR scope: only single oscillating neutron star simulation; lacks testing on binary black holes/binary neutron stars and advanced NR methods (AMR, spectral solvers)
Fundamental error accumulation: lossy compression with minimum ~10⁻⁹ error; geodesic rollouts diverge significantly, especially for chaotic Kerr orbits, limiting long-horizon predictions

Unresolved coordinate dependence: accuracy varies 3 orders of magnitude by coordinate system (Table 8: Cartesian KS 1.37e-5 vs Eddington-Finkelstein 9.21e-9), contradicting coordinate-independence claims and lacking theoretical explanation
Insufficient comparison with alternatives: no benchmarking against spectral methods (claimed 1000–5000× faster) or other compression techniques, making practical advantage unclear
Precision requirements: requires FLOAT64; query time ~ms for 10⁵ points; sequential applications prohibitive; practical deployment barriers underexplored
No time-evolution demonstration: all experiments on single time-slices; unclear if training required per-snapshot or how to amortize training cost in production workflows
Theoretical gaps: no convergence analysis, error bounds, or principled justification for why neural fields suit tensor fields; hyperparameter sensitivity under-explored

strengths: Novel application of neural fields to tensor field representation in numerical relativity with clear technical motivation
Rigorous mathematical treatment of differential geometry and proper implementation of automatic differentiation for computing curvature tensors
Comprehensive experimental validation on canonical GR solutions (Schwarzschild, Kerr, linearized gravity) across multiple coordinate systems
Proof-of-concept demonstration on realistic numerical relativity simulation (oscillating neutron star) with ~160M collocation points
Exceptional compression ratios (4000×) with 5-7 decimal place accuracy and 5 orders of magnitude improvement in derivative accuracy over finite differencing
Outstanding presentation quality with extensive mathematical exposition, detailed appendices, and reproducibility specifications
Practical benefits demonstrated: mesh-agnosticity, continuous querying at arbitrary resolution, native support for automatic differentiation
weaknesses: Severely limited scope of realistic applications: only one numerical relativity simulation tested; no validation on binary black hole/neutron star mergers or production NR workflows that are most computationally critical

Fundamental floating-point precision limitations: lossy compression even with FLOAT64 training, long-time trajectory integration divergence (Figure 16), and FLOAT64 requirement for geodesic solvers severely limit applicability to dynamic time-stepped simulations

Query time overhead inadequately addressed: millisecond-scale queries (Figure 23) for sequential operations; no end-to-end wall-clock time comparison vs. traditional approaches, making total computational benefit unclear

Dramatic coordinate system sensitivity undermines claimed coordinate-agnosticism: accuracy varies 3 orders of magnitude across coordinates (Table 8); no principled guidance for coordinate selection, requiring manual intervention
Missing critical comparisons: no evaluation against standard compression methods (ZIP, HDF5), other ML-based compression, tensor decomposition, or spectral methods mentioned as 1000-5000× faster

Limited machine learning algorithmic novelty: uses standard MLPs with standard activations; Sobolev training is prior work; SOAP optimizer is concurrent work; contribution is primarily application of existing techniques
Insufficient scalability analysis: training time scaling unclear, memory requirements during training not specified, compression ratio behavior with increased resolution not characterized
Theoretical understanding lacking: no formal justification for why neural fields suit tensor fields, no approximation bounds or convergence analysis, connection to Neural Tensor Fields underdeveloped

Time-evolution validation insufficient: most validation on single time slices; geodesic tests show concerning long-term divergence; no tests of whether method preserves differential geometric structure under dynamics
